nameStory: The fan pelt lichen gets its name from its distinctive fan-shaped lobes that spread out like a hand-held fan or a peacock's tail. Like other pelt lichens, it resembles a thin animal hide or pelt laid flat against its growing surface, giving this whole group their common name.
description: Fan pelt lichen is a leafy, foliose lichen that forms flat, spreading patches on soil and rocks. Its rounded to fan-shaped lobes measure about half an inch wide and create an overlapping pattern reminiscent of scales or shingles. This lichen dramatically changes color with moisture - appearing deep green when wet and shifting to dark grey-green when dry. It's a medium-sized lichen that can form patches several inches across.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy patches with rounded to fan-shaped lobes that overlap like shingles, each lobe about 10-15mm wide

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Deep green when wet, transforming to dark grey-green when dry - this color change is quite dramatic

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth to the touch, while the underside is white with distinctive raised black veins that feel bumpy

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Nearly always has round, flat, reddish-brown fruiting bodies (apothecia) that look like tiny saucers

habitat: Fan pelt lichen grows on soil, mossy ground, and sometimes rocks in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests and woodlands. Look for it in deciduous and mixed forests, particularly in areas with good moisture retention like north-facing slopes or near streams. It prefers areas with clean air and can be found from lowland forests up into mountainous regions.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when it shows its deep green coloration. Look for the contrast between wet green patches and dry grey-green areas.
seasonality.summer: Often appears grey-green during dry periods, but summer thunderstorms will quickly transform it to bright green within minutes of getting wet.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for identification as fall rains keep it hydrated and green, while the reddish-brown fruiting bodies contrast nicely with fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round under snow, appearing grey-green when exposed. Winter moisture from snow melt can trigger the dramatic color change to green.

funFact: Fan pelt lichen can change from dull grey-green to vibrant deep green in just minutes when it gets wet - you can actually watch this magical transformation happen in real-time if you spray it with water!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pelt lichens, but fan pelt lichen's distinctive raised black veins on the white underside set it apart. Memory trick: flip it over and look for the 'black highway system' - those raised veins are like roads on a map that you can feel with your finger.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fan lichen' in some sources, the more widely accepted common name is 'fan pelt lichen' to distinguish it from other fan-shaped lichens and to emphasize its membership in the pelt lichen family.
compareHints: Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath. Dog pelt lichen has a more textured, fuzzy upper surface, while scaly pelt lichen has obvious scales or granules on top. The consistently present reddish-brown fruiting bodies also help distinguish it from relatives that fruit less reliably.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
